Who's driving the Dubai Metro?
Nobody. The Dubai Metro is driverless: computers drive every train, and each one keeps a moving bubble of empty track around it.
A control room watches the whole network day and night, and 99.7% of trips run on time.

Send this to someone who still looks for the driver.

Sources: Gulf News, Guinness World Records, Dubai Media Office.

Where does Dubai's tap water come from?
The sea. The salt comes out in one of two ways: boil the water and catch the steam, or squeeze it through a membrane that stops over 99% of the salt.
Then minerals go back in, so it tastes right and is kind to the pipes.

Sources: UAE Government portal u.ae, IEEE TechNav, USGS.

What's holding up Palm Jumeirah?
Sand and rock. No concrete, no steel.
An 11 km rock crescent went in first, then ships sprayed about 94 million cubic metres of sand into place, guided by GPS. Then the sand was vibrated tight so it can't act like a liquid in a quake.

Got a lesh? Comment it, we'll explain it.

Sources: Gulf News, Royal IHC, Arabian Business.

Can a number plate cost more than the car?
Plate P 7 sold for 55 million dirhams at a charity auction in Dubai in 2023.
One digit makes it rare, and Guinness World Records calls it the most expensive number plate ever sold.
All of it went to feed people in need. Lesh wins, Akeed owes a karak.

Next argument, you pick. Comment A or B.
A: Akeed says tap water here comes from a well.
B: Akeed says bus stops here never have air conditioning.

Sources: Guinness World Records, Khaleej Times.

See this 10 digit sign by your building's door?
It's not a random serial number. It's called Makani, Arabic for "my location", and the digits come from the map coordinates of the entrance, accurate to about a metre. Big buildings get one for every entrance.
So instead of "turn left at the big palm tree", you just send ten digits. Taxis can use it, and so can emergency teams. Ajman, Fujairah, Ras Al Khaimah and Umm Al Quwain use it too.

Send this to the friend who still gives directions by landmarks.

Sources: Dubai Municipality, Gulf News, The National, Emirates 24/7.

Why pay 55 million dirhams for a number plate?
Because it has one digit. A Dubai plate can have up to five, so a single digit plate is as rare as plates get.
In 2023 plate P 7 sold for AED 55 million at a charity auction in Dubai, a Guinness World Records title. All of it went to a food aid fund.

Sources: Guinness World Records, Khaleej Times, RTA.

Some Dubai bus stops come with their own air conditioned room.
But they have to earn it. Dubai's roads authority sorts its shelters into four types by riders a day. More than 750 a day makes a main stop, and main stops get a cooled waiting room plus shaded seats outside. Fewer riders? Just shade.
The new shelters also get a screen with the bus map and times, and a space kept for wheelchairs. By April 2026, 726 were finished, for a bus network that carries over 192 million riders a year.

Send this to the friend who says nobody takes the bus in Dubai.

Sources: Dubai Media Office, RTA, Gulf News, Khaleej Times.

Your DEWA bill doesn't have one price. It has four.
DEWA charges electricity in four slabs: green, yellow, orange and red. On a standard home, your first 2,000 units a month cost 23 fils each. The next 2,000 cost 28, then 32, and every unit past 6,000 costs 38.
Now add summer. DEWA says air conditioning takes about 60% of the power at peak times, so your extra units land in the pricey slabs. A fuel surcharge and 5% VAT come on top. DEWA's tip: set your AC to 24 degrees.

Send this to the friend who keeps it on 18.

Sources: DEWA, Dubai Executive Council Resolution 16 of 2011, Gulf News.
